ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Referral — Josephine Baker — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Establishing care three weeks after a heart attack and stent, with breathlessness on exertion and tiredness: examination, ECG, laboratory tests, medicines, mood screening, cardiac rehabilitation and the chest-pain action plan

text.paragraph: Breathlessness and tiredness three weeks after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery, in a 62-year-old woman. Please assess the cause of the breathlessness and her heart function, review her antiplatelet therapy and other medicines, and advise on cardiac rehabilitation and a return to performing on stage. [S]
Urgency: Soon; on the day of her two-week visit, after the echocardiogram that morning. [S]

list.item: What is causing her breathlessness: reduced heart function, ongoing ischemia, a medicine effect, or deconditioning?
What does the echocardiogram show, and does she need further testing now?
Is ticagrelor the right P2Y12 inhibitor for her, and for how long should she take dual antiplatelet therapy?
Do you agree with metoprolol and lisinopril, and what blood pressure and LDL targets do you advise, given her lipoprotein(a) result?
When and how can she return to singing and dancing on stage, and does she need an exercise test first?
How should her hysterectomy and possible early menopause, and her sex, change our approach to her risk?

text.paragraph: Singer and dancer, decorated veteran and civil rights activist, under heavy financial strain after the recent loss of her home and estate; mother of twelve adopted children. Pressure in the chest that she first took for strain, with admission the next morning to a regional hospital: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, 90% stenosis of the mid right coronary artery treated with one drug-eluting stent, mild disease elsewhere; LDL 146 mg/dL and high blood pressure found during the stay. Discharged on aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate 25 mg, lisinopril 5 mg and nitroglycerin as needed. Since discharge, breathlessness on one flight of stairs and tiredness, without chest pain. Today: blood pressure 138/84, pulse 64, oxygen saturation 98%; lungs clear; no edema. ECG: sinus rhythm, small inferior Q waves, no acute change. Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, platelets 264, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL (eGFR 81), potassium 4.4 mmol/L, LDL 84 mg/dL after three weeks of atorvastatin, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%. PHQ-9 7, with no thoughts of self-harm. Never smoker. A long illness in her thirties after the loss of a pregnancy, reportedly with an emergency hysterectomy; whether the ovaries were removed is not known. Enrolled in cardiac rehabilitation today. Lipoprotein(a) ordered. She asks to be listened to and to have each medicine explained [S]

list.item: She wants to return to the stage and to have the strength to care for her children. [S]
She is afraid of another heart attack and of what would happen to her family. [S]
Debts and lost income make every cost a worry. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: She was born Freda Josephine McDonald on June 3, 1906, in St. Louis, Missouri, to Carrie McDonald and Eddie Carson, into a family with little money. [D]
She grew up in poor neighborhoods of St. Louis and began working as a child; she married twice before the age of 16 and kept the surname of her second husband, William Howard Baker. [D]

She danced in New York in the musicals Shuffle Along and The Chocolate Dandies, came to Paris with her troupe in 1925 to perform at the Théâtre des Champs-Elysées, and became the most famous and highest-paid American performer in France. [D]
She married a Frenchman in 1937 and became a French citizen; the National Park Service gives 1936. [D]

During the Second World War she worked for the intelligence services of Free France with the rank of sub-lieutenant, gathering information and carrying messages written in invisible ink on her sheet music; on August 18, 1961, she received the Legion of Honor and the Croix de guerre with palm. [D]

She bought a château at Les Milandes in the Périgord, where she made a "village of the world" and raised twelve children of different nationalities and religions whom she had adopted during her tours with Jo Bouillon, her husband; the children were called the "Rainbow Tribe". [D]

In North Africa during the war she was taken urgently to hospital in Casablanca, where she stayed in bed from June 1941 to December 1942, had five operations and was several times reported to be dying; she continued her intelligence work from her room. [D]

The illness followed the loss of a pregnancy in 1941, given as a stillbirth in Casablanca by one source and as a miscarriage by another; the second account says a severe infection required a hysterectomy, after which she developed peritonitis and septicemia. La Croix says she was unable to have children. [R]
At the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August 28, 1963, she was one of the few women to speak; she came in her military uniform with her decorations. [D]

Les Milandes ran into heavy debt; she toured repeatedly to pay it, and on June 2, 1964, she made a televised appeal for donations, saying her work no longer covered debts of about 200 million old francs. [D]

In March 1969, after a court ordered her eviction, she was removed from the château and sat for seven hours in the rain on its steps; she had a new heart attack and ended the day in hospital in Périgueux. Les Milandes was sold at auction that year. [D]

list.item: Entertainer, singer and dancer for more than forty years, in Paris and on tours around the world; has stopped performing while she recovers and wants to return to the stage [S]
Veteran of the wartime Resistance, decorated for intelligence work, and a civil rights activist who has spoken against segregation all her life [S]
Mother of twelve adopted children, some still at school; the family recently lost the home and estate where she raised them, and now lives in a rented house [S]
Finances: large debts from the estate; income only from performing, which has stopped since the heart attack; she is anxious about the cost of medicines and of the children's needs [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: rarely, a glass of champagne on occasion. No drug use [S]
Diet: irregular meals around rehearsals and travel, often late at night; enjoys cooking for her family; little salt added [S]

Says she waited until the morning to go to hospital, thinking the pressure in her chest was the strain of the eviction; asks that her account of her body be taken seriously and that she be told plainly what each medicine is for [S]

Respectful, trauma-informed shared decisions: take her account of her symptoms seriously, explain each medicine and its reason plainly, write the plan down, and check costs with her before prescribing. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); Acute Myocardial Infarction in Women: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2016); Sex and Race/Ethnicity-Related Disparities in Care and Outcomes After Hospitalization for Coronary Artery Disease Among Older Adults (2016) [S]

Dual antiplatelet therapy, aspirin 81 mg with a P2Y12 inhibitor, for twelve months from the heart attack, never stopped without speaking to cardiology; then aspirin alone. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease and acute myocardial infarction monographs (2026) [S]

Atorvastatin 80 mg daily; lipid panel four to eight weeks after the start; goal LDL below 70 mg/dL with at least a 50% fall; lipoprotein(a) measured once. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease and acute myocardial infarction monographs (2026) [S]

Metoprolol succinate for at least the first year after the heart attack; lisinopril for high blood pressure, with home readings and a target below 130/80 mmHg; potassium and creatinine one to two weeks after any dose change. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease and acute myocardial infarction monographs (2026) [S]

Enroll in a 36-session outpatient cardiac rehabilitation program, starting within two weeks, with exercise training, nutrition, stress management and psychological support; the clinic will call her if she misses sessions. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); Acute Myocardial Infarction in Women: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2016); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, ischemic heart disease and acute myocardial infarction monographs (2026) [S]

Depression after a heart attack: PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 today, repeat PHQ-9 at about twelve weeks, the rehabilitation program's psychologist, and a lower threshold for treatment if symptoms rise. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); Depression and Coronary Heart Disease: Recommendations for Screening, Referral, and Treatment: A Science Advisory From the American Heart Association (2008); Depression as a Risk Factor for Poor Prognosis Among Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2014) [S]

Chest-pain action plan: nitroglycerin under the tongue, and 911 if pain is not better five minutes after the first tablet; warning symptoms in women, such as breathlessness, unusual tiredness, nausea or jaw, back or arm discomfort, explained. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); Acute Myocardial Infarction in Women: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2016) [S]

Costs: generic medicines in 90-day fills, the clinic social worker for debt advice and help with medicine costs, and rehabilitation sessions at times that fit her family. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023) [S]

Women's cardiovascular risk: record the hysterectomy of her thirties and a possible early menopause as a risk-enhancing factor; hormone therapy is not used to prevent heart disease. Guideline: Acute Myocardial Infarction in Women: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2016); Menopause Transition and Cardiovascular Disease Risk: Implications for Timing of Early Prevention: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association (2020) [S]
